Chapter 4: Becoming a Judge and Shaping the Law
Imagine spending years as a passionate advocate—fighting for what you believe in—and then stepping into a new role where your job isn’t to convince, but to decide. That’s exactly what happened when Ruth was appointed to the federal bench. The shift from advocate to judge wasn’t easy. Suddenly, she had to set her personal views aside and focus on applying the law as fairly as possible, even when it challenged her own beliefs.
Ruth handled this transition with the same careful dedication that had defined her entire career. She read every brief, weighed every argument, and made sure her opinions were not just thorough, but crystal clear. If you’ve ever tried to write something that’s both precise and easy to understand, you know just how much work that can be.
On the bench, Ruth earned a reputation for being deeply collegial. She listened—really listened—to her colleagues, and looked for common ground wherever she could find it. But here’s the thing: she never compromised her core principles. If she disagreed with a decision, she didn’t just grumble about it. She explained her reasoning thoughtfully and respectfully, always hoping to persuade others—or at the very least, to lay the groundwork for future change.
One thing that set Ruth apart was the way she focused on the real-world impact of the law. She never lost sight of how decisions would actually affect people’s lives—especially those who were often overlooked. For Ruth, the law wasn’t just a collection of rules. It was a tool for justice. And that perspective earned her respect, even from folks who didn’t always agree with her.
Ruth’s empathy came, in part, from her own experiences as an outsider. She remembered what it felt like to be excluded—and she brought that understanding to her work. She balanced emotion with reason, always careful not to let one overshadow the other. Her opinions were logical and clear, but they also showed a real awareness of the challenges people faced.
As word of her thoughtful approach spread, so did Ruth’s influence. She became a role model for young lawyers—especially women—who saw in her a path they could follow. She proved that you could be both principled and pragmatic, that you could keep fighting for change while also knowing when to compromise.
In so many ways, Ruth’s work as a judge paved the way for her future on the Supreme Court, where her impact would only grow stronger.
